name: Victor Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Greenway co-op farm by five for morning milking, a hundred and ten cows in the old herringbone parlour. After that it's scraping yards, feeding calves, and in summer I'm on the maize, mostly carting and helping with silage. I drove a forklift in a warehouse for twenty-two years, so at 56 I came here as the new boy, and I'm still the new boy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the co-op is owned by the members, me included, even if my share is tiny. Every quarter there's a meeting and you can stand up and say something. What wears me out is the early starts and the pay, which is the lowest rate on the farm, and with Salma's care home wages we're still only just covering things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that fuss for a better spell-checker. At the co-op the office might use it for the milk records and that's it. I'd probably post a joke about it on the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same life we have now, which is tight. The co-op is steady and nobody's talking about cutting staff, so I don't lose sleep over the job. It's the money that bothers me, we've got about three weeks saved and the boiler is twenty years old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the milking and try to get my artificial insemination certificate, which the co-op pays for, so I'm worth a bit more an hour. I'd put forty a month aside for the boiler. And I'd keep using the phone assistant now and then to look up calf problems, the way I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled about the job, nervous about the boiler. That sounds silly, but that's the honest picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the boiler goes this winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the boiler goes this winter, we borrow from Salma's sister again, like we did for the car tyres. I hate doing it, but she's good about it. That's why the forty a month matters, so we don't keep going back to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use an AI assistant now and then. What for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring I had a calf with scours and the vet was out on another call, so I asked the phone what to watch for. It told me about fluids and keeping her warm, which Mehmet the herdsman had already told me, but it helped me feel less stupid. I don't trust it with anything big.

say: I'd joke that it was **all that fuss** for a better spell-checker.
I'd say the co-op office might use it for **milk records** and not much else.
think: The co-op job feels **steady**, so I don't lose sleep over the work.
Money is the real worry: **three weeks** saved and a twenty-year-old **boiler**.
do: Get the **AI certificate** for cattle breeding, which the co-op pays for, to earn more an hour.
Put **forty a month** aside for the boiler.
Keep using the phone assistant **now and then** for calf problems.
feel: **Settled** about the job but **nervous** about the boiler.
S0.quote: If the boiler goes this winter, we borrow from Salma's sister again, like we did for the car tyres.
fieldNote: He feels the **co-op** protects his job, so his worry centres on **household money**.
He uses AI only as a **second opinion**, after the herdsman has already told him.
Borrowing from family is the **fallback** he's ashamed of and wants to stop.

steps.text: Get the cattle insemination certificate the co-op pays for
Put forty a month aside for the old boiler

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people and the young ones who need help now, not so much us in the parlour. At the co-op meeting I'd stand up and ask what the plan is for Joanna in the office if the software does her ordering. Online I'd share stuff about retraining money from the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly fine for a few years. Nobody's going to code their way into milking a cow, but my daughter answers phones for an energy company, and that's exactly the list on your card. My son Karim is a junior accountant in the city, so he's on the list too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the co-op for a short course on the herd software, so if the planning goes digital I'm the one who can read it. I'd push at the members' meeting for a written promise that nobody gets let go without retraining first. And I'd tell Amina to start looking at nursing or something with people now, while she's got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like watching weather come in over the hill when your own field's still dry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Amina, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, the phone job is going to get thin, so start the evening course at the college this year and don't wait to be pushed. She'd say Dad, you sound like a news report. But I worked twenty-two years at a warehouse and watched the scanners come in, so I know how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your job is fine for a few years. Then you're taking a software course. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. The cows still need a person this year, but the co-op will want someone to read the screens when the planning goes digital, and I'd rather that's me than some lad from town. Being steady doesn't mean sitting still.

say: I'd say **office workers** and young people need help first, not us in the parlour.
I'd ask at the **co-op meeting** what happens to Joanna if software does the ordering.
think: Nobody will **code their way** into milking a cow, so I'm fine for a few years.
My kids are the worry: Karim in **accounting** and Amina on a **phone line**.
do: Ask the co-op for a short course on the **herd software**.
Push for a **written promise** that nobody goes without retraining first.
Tell Amina to start an **evening course** at the college this year.
feel: **Uneasy**, like weather coming in while my own **field** is still dry.
S1.quote: Nobody's going to code their way into milking a cow, but my daughter answers phones for an energy company, and that's exactly the list on your card.
fieldNote: He sees his own **hands-on job** as safe for now and his **children's jobs** as exposed.
His years at a warehouse when scanners came in shape his **clear-eyed** view.
He uses the co-op's **democracy** as his main tool, asking for written promises on retraining.

steps.text: Ask the co-op for a course on the herd software
Push the members' meeting for a no-layoffs-without-retraining promise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in fast, a wage guarantee or something, because two years is nothing. At the co-op I'd say, we own this place, so we decide together how the robots come in. Online I'd be sharing every union and co-op statement I could find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the computers taking the planning in 2028 doesn't scare me, I barely touch it. But robots in 2031, when I'm 63, could do the milking, and robotic milkers already exist, the big farm on the ridge has two. The difference is we're a co-op, so maybe the members vote to keep people on, but I'm the newest and the slowest, so I can't count on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get on the co-op's working group for new technology, so I'm in the room. I'd ask to be trained on the robotic milking units before they arrive, cleaning, fixing the arms, checking alarms. I'd stop the takeaways and cut the phone plans to save sixty a month, and I'd ask Karim if he could help with the boiler if it comes to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not helpless. My stomach goes tight, and then I think, at least I can stand up at a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at that first members' meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we all bought into this co-op so the money stays with the people who work the land. If robots save the co-op wages, then the savings should pay for the workers they replace until pension age. Some of the older members would clap and some of the younger ones would look at their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does asking Karim feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. A father should be giving, not asking. But if AGI is taking accountant jobs in 2028, Karim might be in a worse spot than me, so I might not ask at all. That's the bit that keeps me awake, honestly.

say: I'd say the government needs a **wage guarantee** fast, because **two years** is nothing.
I'd tell the co-op that **we own** this place, so we decide how robots come in.
think: Robots in **2031** could do the milking when I'm 63 and still the **newest hand**.
The co-op might vote to keep people on, but **I can't count** on it.
do: Join the co-op's **technology working group** to be in the room.
Ask to be trained on **robotic milking** units before they arrive.
Cut takeaways and phone plans to save **sixty a month**.
feel: **Anxious** but **not helpless**, because I can still stand up at a meeting.
S2.quote: If robots save the co-op wages, then the savings should pay for the workers they replace until pension age.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as time to get trained on the robots before they reach the parlour.
His **co-op membership** gives him a sense of control many hired hands lack.
He worries his son's **accountancy job** goes first, which may close the family fallback.

steps.text: Join the co-op's working group on new machines
Get trained on cleaning and fixing robotic milking units
Stop takeaways and cut phone plans to save sixty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's use it, and I'd say it at the co-op meeting before anyone else does. I'd tell friends at the mosque that this is the time to get the kids into trades. Online I'd share stuff pushing the government to fund retraining now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2034 means I'm 66, so I'm working alongside them for maybe a year before I stop. That I can live with. The bigger thing is AGI in 2031 taking Karim's accounting and Amina's phone work, because that's my children's whole working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the robotic milking course at the agricultural college in the next couple of years, while the co-op is still deciding what to buy. I'd write to our local representative about funding retraining for farm workers. And I'd try to get the forty a month for the boiler up to sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can work with. Five years is enough to get my boots under the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the college course and not wait for the co-op to train you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I've got the paper already, I'm the obvious choice when the robots come, not the one they work around. The course is evenings, two nights a week, and Salma says she'll drive me if the car's playing up. I learned the forklift scanners at forty-five, so I can learn robotic milking at sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Karim?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to start moving toward the side of accounting where you sit with people, the advising, because a machine adding up numbers is the first thing to go. He'd probably already know that better than me. Still, a dad says it.

say: I'd call five years a **fair warning** and say so at the co-op first.
I'd tell friends at the mosque this is the time to get kids into **trades**.
think: Robots in **2034** leave me working beside them for about a year before I stop.
AGI in 2031 hits my **children's** whole working lives harder than mine.
do: Sign up for the evening **robotic milking course** at the agricultural college.
Write to our local representative about **retraining funds** for farm workers.
Raise boiler savings from forty to **sixty a month**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but with enough time to get my boots under the table.
S3.quote: I learned the forklift scanners at forty-five, so I can learn robotic milking at sixty.
fieldNote: Five years turns the robots into something he can **prepare for** rather than fear.
His past at the warehouse gives him **confidence** about learning new machines.
His real worry moves to his **children**, whose desk jobs face AGI first.

steps.text: Take the evening robotic milking course at the agricultural college
Write to the local representative about farm worker retraining
Raise the boiler savings from forty to sixty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for governments to get ready, so if they don't, it's on them. At the co-op I'd say we should start a fund now for workers who'll be replaced. Online I'd probably keep my head down, it would feel far off to most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039 means I'm long retired, 71, so the farm job is mine until I stop at 67. What stays is the money: low pay, a small pension and the house needing work. That and the kids, of course, because ten years is their problem, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and do the insemination certificate so I earn a bit more these last years. I'd keep using the phone assistant now and then, maybe for the herd records too. I'd push the co-op to start a transition fund, even a small one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty easy about the job, a bit heavy about everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the transition fund look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit off every litre, maybe half a penny, put into a pot for retraining. Half a penny off every litre, put into a pot for ten years, becomes real money when the machines come. Mehmet would say it's a waste, but Mehmet's 41 and he'll be glad of it in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would change your mind and make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big farm on the ridge started letting people go, I'd take it seriously quicker. Seeing it next door is different from hearing about it. Until then I'd be steady, like always.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so if governments don't prepare, **it's on them**.
I'd tell the co-op to start a **fund** now for workers who'll be replaced.
think: Robots in **2039** come after I retire at 67, so the farm job is **mine** until then.
The money worries stay: **low pay**, a small pension and a house needing work.
do: Carry on and finish the **insemination certificate** to earn more in my last years.
Push the co-op to start a small **transition fund**.
feel: **Easy** about the job but **heavy** about everything else.
S4.quote: Half a penny off every litre, put into a pot for ten years, becomes real money when the machines come.
fieldNote: With a decade, he sees the job as safe until **retirement**, but money keeps him **uneasy**.
His co-op **transition fund** idea is the most concrete policy thought in the interview.
He'd only act sooner if he saw **layoffs next door**, which fits his steady nature.

steps.text: Finish the cattle insemination certificate to earn more an hour
Propose a half-penny-a-litre transition fund at the co-op

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots could reach our parlour at 63 and the planning goes even sooner. What would help is training on the robotic milking before it arrives, paid for by the co-op or the government, and a bridge to my pension if I still get pushed out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about who owns the machines. When a co-op owns the robot, the workers can share the savings. When a big company owns it, the savings go somewhere else, and that's the whole difference.

headlineQuote: When a co-op owns the robot, the workers can share the savings.
portrait: Victor is 58, a former **forklift driver** now the newest milker on a co-op dairy and maize farm.
He and his wife Salma, a care home worker, have about **three weeks** saved and an ageing boiler.
He uses AI **now and then** and believes he can learn robotic milking as he learned warehouse scanners.
He trusts the **co-op's** members' meetings to give him a voice, and wants savings from robots shared.
He worries more about his **children's desk jobs** than his own hands-on work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots could reach the milking parlour when he's 63.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training** on robotic milking before it arrives.
A **bridge payment** to his pension if he's still pushed out.
